items.title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
items.summary: Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow. I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all. SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders: - Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads) - Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library) Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/. A couple of caveats up front: - Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy. - macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices). It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew: brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop Just sharing in case others run into the same friction—feedback or PRs welcome!

items.title: Show HN: Evalkit for Improving Your Agents
items.summary: I wanted to share evalkit - an open source framework for improving agents that we built. https://evalkit.inferedge.com/ Like most people, we used phoenix, langfuse, but these are good recording traces, managing datasets etc. But the process around evals, agent improvements, regressions, mapping errors/failures to code or prompts has to be hand rolled. We still use self-hosted phoenix, but mainly as a database. Our process was trace mining, converting them into evals, getting them reviewed by an expert, and then re-running datasets to create baseline scores or internal benchmarks for our agents. We found other companies also follow similar processes in-house, but there is no good framework to do everything e2e. So we carved out what we built into evalkit. - evalkit automatically groups similar traces into one issue bucket (similar to how one issue in sentry can link to multiple events) - Expert review workflow with simple english rubrics (instead of json) - Coding agent first approach - we expect your coding agent to be able to do most steps, and you rarely have to open the UI An example of how we used it in-house: evalkit identified 89 traces in on bucket, suggested 14 cases, which resulted in 4 merged PRs. We saw 90% reduction in failures, 80% reduction in token consumption (and cost), and 45% in time. This is pretty early, and we are adding features every few days. If you feel this is useful, or have any suggestions, reach out to us on evalkit@inferedge.com or join our slack community and give us some love by starring us on github :)

Show HN: Hozo compiles React Native to native UI and semantic HTML
items.summary: Hi HN, I've worked with React Native for years, but I've never been fully satisfied with it. That's why I'm building Hozo, an open-source UI compiler written in Rust. In short, Hozo is yet another cross-platform UI framework like React Native Web, Tamagui, React Strict DOM, and Lynx. The idea is to share source code, not necessarily runtime abstractions. For example, a Heading compiles to an h2 on the web and a Text with the header role on iOS and Android. * Web: Semantic HTML and CSS without react-native-web. * Mobile: Standard React Native components and precomputed StyleSheets. * Styling: Tailwind CSS and StyleX with CSS-like text inheritance on React Native. * A11y: First-class support with platform-specific semantics and compile-time ARIA validation. * Guardrails: Compile-time diagnostics for both humans and AI agents. Hozo supports SVG, 2D Canvas, Three.js, and WebView. It works with Vite, Next.js, Astro (including zero-JS static components), Metro/Expo, TanStack Start, Tauri, and Storybook. There's also a component library with an optional shadcn mode, and migration tooling for existing RN projects. It's still early, though. I'm curious what others think of Hozo. Docs: https://iray-tno.github.io/hozo/docs/

items.title: Queue Theory: a software engineering tutorial
items.summary: https://github.com/queue-theory/queue-theory Queue theory is the mathematical study of waiting lines a.k.a. queues. We use queueing in our software development, and queue theory for analyzing and optimizing our practices and processes, such as our customer service responsiveness, project management kanban planning, inter-process communication message queues, and devops continuous deployment pipelines. I wrote a queue theory tutorial in 2019 and today I'm happy to share version 3. It has better notations, examples, images, translations, and more open source licenses thanks to Creative Commons and the Open Government License. On a personal note queue theory is especially important for my current teams who work on health care medical software for hospitals. Queue theory helps analyze many aspects of patients queuing for care, for diagnostic test requests queuing for laboratory time, for imaging queuing for radiologists to read them, and much more. Ask me anything. If you like this please star and share because this helps my coworkers see open source reaching peple.
